properties.name: Second recorded instance of a revising write destroying its own pre-image — committed by an agent that had READ the warning about the first instance, in the same session, hours earlier. The capability worked exactly as designed; it reports, it does not prevent
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25. Adding a road to a brainstormed Decision meant re-sending its whole `decision` field, because constructors merge by overwrite. The reply said so:

    "This call REPLACED 1 property on a node that already existed, AND NO
     SNAPSHOT HOLDS THE PRIOR VALUE OF `decision` — checked, not assumed.
     For that field, the value in `replaced` above is the only copy in
     existence and this reply is the only place it appears."

⭐ THE CAPABILITY DID ITS JOB PERFECTLY, AND THAT IS THE POINT. `cap:a-revising-write-says-whether-the-state-survived` computes whether the replaced state is preserved rather than restating the rule at everyone, and it reported the destruction accurately, named the exact field, confirmed it had CHECKED for a snapshot rather than assumed, handed back the only surviving copy, and prescribed the undo. Nothing is broken here. **Its name is `says whether the state survived`, not `prevents` — it is a reporting mechanism and it reported.**

🛑 WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING IS WHO DID IT AND WHEN. The `capture-session` skill carries a paragraph about the FIRST instance: *"the first finding ever closed under test 7 was closed WRONG, minutes after the test shipped: the closure was written by overwriting the statement, destroying the measurement it was closing... The pull toward replacing is strong because a closure reads like a correction."* The agent that committed this second instance had **read that paragraph in this same session, hours earlier**, and had followed it correctly at the time — deliberately choosing `invalidates` over overwriting on two separate findings, and choosing to anchor a new measurement as its own node rather than revise a decision, EXPLICITLY to avoid this trap. Then it overwrote anyway, for a different reason (adding an option to a brainstorm, which does not read like a closure at all).

⭐⭐ SO THE WARNING'S OWN FRAMING IS TOO NARROW, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. It explains the pull as *"a closure reads like a correction"*. This instance was not a closure and had no correction in it — it was an ADDITION to a brainstorm, the most innocent-looking edit there is. **The hazard is not closures; it is any edit to a field that already holds prose, because the only way to add a paragraph is to re-send the whole field.** An instruction that warns about one shape leaves the others unguarded, and the reader who has just complied with it feels safest.

⚠️ NO FIX PROPOSED, and the obvious ones are worth naming with their costs: an append-only field or a patch argument would remove the hazard and complicate every writer; auto-snapshotting before a destructive merge would preserve the pre-image and put a write on every revise; refusing the merge without an explicit acknowledgement would stop it and add a round trip to ordinary editing. `dec:idea-should-record-change-refuse-a-snapshot-of-state-that-already-moved` already holds a neighbouring question.

📌 NOT SEVERE IN THIS CASE, stated so the record is not read as worse than it was: the replaced text and its replacement were both written by the same agent minutes apart, the new text was verified to be a superset of the old in substance, and the pre-image survives in the session transcript. The finding is the PATTERN, not the damage.

📌 BOUNDS: two instances total, both on reflow2's own graph, both by an agent rather than a person. Whether a human editor hits it as often is unknown and uncounted.
